conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you so much for being here today. My name is Dr. Martinez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives.

Today I’ll be walking you through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a well-trusted tool that screens for depressive and anxiety symptoms, and it includes one question about self-harm risk. The goal is simply to get a snapshot of how you’ve been feeling over the past week so we can make sure you have the support you deserve.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within our treatment team. There are no right or wrong answers, and this isn’t a test of your parenting—just a way for us to listen to your experience in a safe, judgment-free space. We’ll go through ten questions; most moms finish in about five minutes.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft exhale, eyes a little downcast]

Not really… I mean, I can still smile if someone makes a joke, but it feels forced. Most of the time I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

Not very often… maybe once or twice when my husband sent me a silly meme, but even then the laugh felt kind of flat and didn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs a little, voice quiet]

Not really… I used to get excited about little things, like my morning coffee or a walk with the stroller, but lately it all just feels like another chore. I still go through the motions, but there’s not much joy in it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to my lap, fingers twisting the edge of my sweatshirt]

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy I keep thinking it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. Even when my partner says he’s just being a normal newborn, I still feel like I must be messing up somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[chews lip, voice shaky]

Yes… I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke, even though he’s fine. Or I’ll lie down and can’t stop picturing horrible things—like what if I drop him, or what if he stops breathing in the night. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t turn the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands in lap, shoulders hunched]

Yeah… it’s like a sudden wave, especially at night. My chest gets tight and I feel like I can’t get enough air, even though nothing’s actually happening. I’ll check the baby monitor three, four times, sure something’s wrong even though he’s sleeping peacefully.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a long breath, eyes glassy]

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs to be fed, laundry’s everywhere, and I just freeze, thinking I’ll never get it all done. I manage enough to keep him safe, but everything else feels impossible.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]

Yes… I lie there listening to the baby breathing on the monitor, and my mind just keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs.” Even when he sleeps a four-hour stretch, I can’t settle. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and then I jolt awake convinced I heard him cry.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, voice thick]

Yeah… most of the day I just feel heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest. I’ll be changing his diaper and tears start coming out of nowhere. I keep thinking I should be grateful—he’s healthy, I wanted this baby so badly—but the sadness is just there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, eyes watering]

Yes… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I sat in the nursery rocking him and suddenly I was sobbing into his blanket, trying to stay quiet so he wouldn’t wake up. I couldn’t even tell my partner why—I just felt overwhelmed and… empty.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks away, voice barely above a whisper]

…once or twice. It flashes through my mind when everything feels too much—like, “what if I just weren’t here?” But I would never act on it; I couldn’t leave my baby. I push the thought away as fast as it comes, but it scares me that it shows up at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery.  
Source: self-report via EPDS-style interview.

Symptoms endorsed (≥75% of items):  
- Marked anhedonia, loss of joy, “flat” affect  
- Daily tearfulness, self-described “heaviness”  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent intrusive “what-if” fears (choking/SIDS) → autonomic arousal (racing heart, chest tightness)  
- Nocturnal hypervigilance → prolonged sleep-onset, early jolting awake  
- Overwhelm/“drowning” with routine tasks; functional freeze  
- Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I weren’t here?”) – no plan or intent reported; protective of infant  

Pattern: Persistent low mood + prominent anxiety/panic symptoms, present most days × ≥2 wk.  
Risk flags: Sleep–mood linkage, guilt cognitions, passive SI, no observable protective supports documented today.

Screening level: High clinical concern for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; safety risk requires urgent follow-up (formal assessment, SI evaluation, support planning).
